name: Mohave
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: The main accent or stress in Mojave normally comes on the last vowel (the last syllable) of the word as it is listed in the dictionary. If some other vowel in a dictionary entry is accented, the dictionary shows an accent mark (') over that vowel. The most common use of accents is in words with the special ending ve, meaning 'the place that'. In these words, the final vowel, e, is not accented -- the accent goes on the vowel in the syllable before the ve ending. [...] Like ve, other Mojave endings [...] are not accented either. The accent stays on the last vowel of a word as it is listed in the dictionary (without added endings), and this accent does not change even when endings are added.
new_statements.citation: Munro, Pamela, Nellie Brown & Judith G. Crawford. 1992. A Mojave Dictionary. UCLA Occasional Papers in Linguistics 10. Los Angeles: Department of Linguistics, UCLA.
new_statements.locator: Pronunciation Notes, pp. 316-317 (PDF pp. 322-323); also The Mojave Alphabet, p. 11 (PDF p. 17)

If some other vowel in a dictionary entry is accented, the dictionary shows an accent mark over that vowel. The…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the final vowel of the citation/dictionary form (noun, or verb stem without its =k/=m and other endings), i.e. on the root/stem-final syllable; prefixes precede it and all suffixal endings (switch-reference/tense =k, =m, -pch, nominalizer -ve, etc.) are unstressed and never attract or shift the stress. Lexical exceptions with non-final stress in the dictionary form are marked with a written accent. In surface words this yields root stress rather than a fixed edge position (final in unsuffixed citation forms, penultimate or earlier once endings are added).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Dictionary says nothing. Crawford 1976 (same directory) reports secondary stress on certain verbal suffixes containing /u/ (-um, -tum, -sum, -kum) and on the reduced 'say' suffix -e, which she attributes to their origin in reduced verb roots (idu: 'be', i'i: 'say').
new_statements.exceptions: Words whose dictionary form is not final-stressed carry a written accent mark; all -ve 'the place that' nominalizations are stressed on the vowel before -ve; p.11: 'In most Mojave words listed in the Dictionary, the last vowel is accented.' Kroeber 1911 (pp.63-65) heard many words as final-accented but others (ka'veik 'south', pa'ya 'all', vi'ka 'seven', a'ha 'water' vs ah'a' 'cottonwood', a've 'rattlesnake' vs ave' 'mouse') as non-final or evenly balanced, and argued the accent is realized mainly as raised pitch (about a major third) rather than intensity.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is framed on the dictionary citation form (word without inflectional endings); explicitly says added endings do not receive or move the accent, so the domain is the stem/root within the morphological word. Pedagogical register (pronunciation guide for learners) but authored by the principal modern describer of Mojave (Munro). Based primarily on one speaker (Nellie Brown), Colorado River Indian Reservation, Parker AZ.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Mojave as spoken on the Colorado River Indian Reservation near Parker, Arizona (primarily one speaker, Nellie Brown); same language as Glottolog moha1256 'Mohave' (ISO mov); no dialect split is recognized in Glottolog. Kroeber 1911 recorded Mohave speakers at Needles/Fort Mojave area.

sources.locator: Pronunciation Notes, pp. 316-317 (PDF pp. 322-323); also The Mojave Alphabet, p. 11 (PDF p. 17)
sources.note: The Mojave Alphabet (p.11): in most words the last vowel is accented; an accent mark is written over accented non-final vowels. Pronunciation Notes (pp.316-317): main accent/stress normally on the last vowel (last syllable) of the word as listed in the dictionary; endings such as -ve 'the place that' and other verb endings are never accented; the accent stays on the last vowel of the dictionary form and does not move when endings are added. Intro (p.4) also notes a short/long vowel contrast in both stressed and unstressed positions.

sources.citation: Kroeber, A. L. 1911. Phonetic Elements of the Mohave Language. University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 10(3): 45-96. Berkeley: The University Press.
sources.note: Section 'Stress and pitch accent' pp.63-65: 'Many Mohave words are to our ears definitely accented on the last syllable' (anya' sun, avi' stone, ipa' man, hamo'k three...); when stress precedes the final it is sometimes well marked (ka'veik, pa'ya, vi'ka) but often 'so evenly balanced that it seems to rest on two syllables'; kymograph pitch measurements show the accented vowel 1-4 tones higher; concludes 'heightened pitch rather than increased stress constitutes the normal accent in Mohave'. Also p.50: 'many words have the accent on other than the ultimate syllable', with slurred final short…

No general stress rule stated.
